name: Carly
tagline: An AI assistant sold as a hosted product, with the usual chat plus context plus integrations shape.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Products in this shape are mostly a good system prompt, a model API key, and a tidy interface, and an agent can reproduce that core in an afternoon. What you will not reproduce in one sitting is the surrounding plumbing: OAuth into whatever tools it connects to, background sync, a mobile client, and the hundred small prompt and UX decisions that make it feel like a product rather than a chat box. If the value here is the interface and the prompting, a personal build gets you most of the way. If it leans on integrations or an accumulated store of your data, the gap widens fast. Treat this verdict as provisional until the product scope is confirmed.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that streams chat from a model API, keeps threads in SQLite, and answers questions over files you drop in.
requirements: An API key for an LLM provider
Node 20 and a machine you are willing to leave running
Willingness to write your own system prompt and iterate on it
Per service OAuth apps if you want any real integrations
whatYouLose: Mobile and desktop clients, so the assistant lives in a browser tab you keep losing
Integrations that already work, versus OAuth flows you get to build and maintain
Prompt tuning someone else did for you, including the guardrails you only notice when they are missing
Anything shared: no team access, no shared context, no history that follows you across devices
Someone else absorbing model API cost changes and provider outages
moatNotes: Thin AI wrappers live or die on interface polish and how many things they already plug into. Neither is technically hard, both are tedious.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the assistant that exists on your phone at 11pm beats the better one running on localhost behind a tunnel you forgot to restart. Paid AI assistants sell the absence of maintenance: keys rotated, models swapped when a better one ships, integrations that keep working after a provider changes its API. A personal build is genuinely fine for personal use, right up until you want it on a second device.
notes: The chat box is a weekend, the habit of actually using it is not.
prompt:
Build a local AI assistant called "Carly Lite". Single user, runs on my machine, no accounts.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 with the App Router and TypeScript
- Tailwind CSS for styling, no component library
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/app.db, schema created on first boot
- Model calls go to an OpenAI compatible chat completions endpoint, base URL and key from .env

Features, in scope:
1. Chat page with streaming responses rendered as markdown, code blocks with copy buttons.
2. Threads in a left sidebar: create, rename, delete, persisted in SQLite with all messages.
3. A settings page storing model name, temperature, and a system prompt in the database, editable in the UI.
4. File context: drag in .txt, .md, or .pdf, chunk to roughly 800 tokens, embed via the embeddings endpoint, store vectors as BLOBs in SQLite, and do cosine similarity in JS at query time. Show which chunks were used under each answer.
5. A /api/ask route that takes a question and returns an answer, so I can curl it from scripts.
6. Export a thread to markdown.

Out of scope, do not build: auth, multi user, billing, telemetry, analytics, Docker, third party vector databases, mobile apps.

Rules:
- Secrets only in .env, ship .env.example with OPENAI_BASE_URL, OPENAI_API_KEY, MODEL, EMBEDDING_MODEL.
- No network calls other than the model provider.
- Handle provider errors visibly in the UI instead of failing silently.
- README with two commands to install and run, and one paragraph on where the data lives.
- Seed one example thread so the UI is not empty on first run.
